source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama (2024, ICLR) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: This is the only matched-budget test of generate-run-critique-repair against plain resampling that was found. When repair cost is counted, gains are modest, differ between data subsets, and are sometimes absent. Pass rates are often equal or higher with plain i.i.d. sampling, especially at small budgets.
numbers: CodeLlama-13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS, temperature 0.8, grid np and nfr in {1,2,5,10,25} x {1,3,5,10}. GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each (up to 20 samples) gave 1.05x the pass@20 baseline. 2 initial samples plus 10 repairs each (up to 22 samples) gave 0.97x the pass@22 baseline. GPT-4 beat the baseline by up to 8% on APPS; GPT-3.5 gains were marginal and only at the largest np.
quote: self-repair is not a silver bullet for code generation
limits: Code tasks with unit tests only. Cost is counted in samples, not tokens. The repair loop has no impasse typing. Fixed-grid self-repair, not an adaptive scheme like NL2GenSym or STARS.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly answered by analogy: a repair loop must beat sampling at the same budget, and it often does not. Spend on diverse first attempts before extra repair rounds. Our G7 test must include a best-of-N arm with the same total tokens.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet (feedback-quality experiments)
finding: The bottleneck of self-repair is the quality of the textual diagnosis, not the repair step. Swapping in feedback from a stronger model beat both the baseline and own-feedback repair at every budget. Human feedback raised repair success much more.
numbers: Human programmer feedback on GPT-4 repairs raised the fraction of repaired programs that pass all tests from 33.3% to 52.6% (1.58x). Boosted feedback (GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback for CodeLlama; GPT-4 feedback for GPT-3.5) beat both comparison arms at all budgets on APPS. Human study was small-scale (the paper says so).
quote: current models are held back by their inability to reliably produce accurate and useful feedback on why the code is wrong
limits: Small human study. Only code. Does not compare typed against untyped feedback.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: what matters is whether the recovery step produces a correct diagnosis. An impasse type only helps if it makes the diagnosis better. Test typed operators by diagnosis accuracy, not by label.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: With a fine-tuned revision model and a verifier, N sequential revisions narrowly beat N parallel samples at equal generation count on MATH. The best split between sequential and parallel depends on question difficulty: easy questions prefer all sequential, hard ones a mix. Picking the split per question beat best-of-N with up to 4x less compute.
numbers: MATH (PaLM 2-S* revision model). Compute-optimal allocation matched best-of-N at 64 generations versus 256 (4x less). About 38% of correct answers were turned into incorrect ones by the naive revision model, so a verifier or majority vote picked the final answer.
quote: outperform the parallel best-of-N baseline using up to 4x less test-time compute
limits: Needs a fine-tuned revision model and a learned verifier or difficulty predictor. Cost counted in generations, not tokens. Math only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: at equal budget a mix of retry and refine can beat pure sampling, but only with a verifier and a difficulty signal. Revising can break a correct answer (38%), so keep the code check as the gate. Adaptive allocation by difficulty is the same idea as firing an impasse operator only when needed.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: All tested models do worse when information arrives in turns than when it is given at once. Most of the drop is unreliability, not lost ability. Models propose answers early, then rely on their own earlier wrong attempts, and answers grow longer. Once they take a wrong turn they do not recover.
numbers: Average drop 39% across six tasks, over 200,000 simulated conversations. Aptitude down 15%, unreliability up 112%. Final answers in sharded conversations are 20 to 300% longer than single-turn answers. Recap and Snowball (restating the facts) cut the deterioration by only about 15 to 20% (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, four tasks).
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Underspecified user instructions, simulated users, not agent loops with tool errors. It does not test a clean restart on the same task against a continued context at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: closest evidence that earlier failed attempts anchor later ones. The authors advise starting a new conversation and consolidating what was learned. It supports a fresh-context subgoal that returns one typed result, but the isolation factor is still not measured on its own.

source: Sun, Lu, Ling et al. (2025) Scaling Long-Horizon LLM Agent via Context-Folding
finding: An agent branches into a sub-trajectory for a subtask and folds it on return, keeping only a short summary of the outcome. With a 32K active window and at most 10 branches it matched or beat a ReAct agent with a 327K window. Branches cannot nest. Training (FoldGRPO, RL) gave most of the gain.
numbers: Seed-OSS-36B. After RL: BrowseComp-Plus (N=150) pass@1 62.0% and SWE-Bench Verified (N=500) 58.0%. RL added +20.0 and +8.8 points. FoldGRPO beat plain GRPO by +7.7 and +1.6 points. Before RL the prompted folding agent beat 32K ReAct and the summary agent but not 327K ReAct. Max total 327,680 tokens, so total tokens were not equal.
quote: creating new branches is disabled while in execution state
limits: Needs RL training; the prompt-only version does not match long-context ReAct. Table text was scrambled in extraction, so the headline numbers come from the paper text. Total tokens differ between arms. Single lab, one model.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10. Isolating a subtask context and returning a short result keeps the main context small, and the design uses depth 1 with a hard branch cap of 10. This is a measured case for a depth cap. It does not isolate anchoring and does not apply to a no-training scaffold.

source: Schroeder, Morgan, Luo, Glass (2025) THREAD: Thinking Deeper with Recursive Spawning
finding: A thread can spawn child threads that return only the tokens the parent needs. If a child fails, the parent reads the feedback, rewrites the subtask and spawns again. Few-shot prompting only, no training. It reports large gains over ReAct, ADaPT and Reflexion on agent tasks.
numbers: ALFWorld combined success, Llama-3-8b: THREAD 71.6 vs ReAct 20.1, ADaPT 30.6, Reflexion 25.4. CodeLlama-7b: 91.0 vs ReAct 23.1. GPT-3.5, 5 runs: ALFWorld 95.7 (SE 0.28), TextCraft 93.7 (0.37), WebShop 48.6 (0.40). Average thread depth 3.6 to 5.8, max depth 6 to 10. Abstract claims gains of 10 to 50 points absolute.
quote: Child threads return only the information needed for the parent to complete its work
limits: No equal-token control, and no cap on depth was tested although max depth reached 10. Ablations (removing variables, full-sequence return, separate thread-0 prompt) are shown as error-count figures. Different base methods use different prompts.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10. A prompt-only recursive subgoal with typed return works across three small models and has run-to-run error bars (5 runs). The parent re-specifying the subtask after a child fails is the same move as an impasse that raises a new subgoal. Still no equal-token comparison.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: The agent induces reusable workflows from past successful runs and supplies them to later tasks. It raised success on web navigation and shortened the runs. The authors state that induced workflows are not always correct and can lower performance, and that offline workflows can mismatch the test distribution.
numbers: Relative success gains of 24.6% on Mind2Web and 51.1% on WebArena (gpt-4, temperature 0; WebArena +12.0 points over BrowserGym). Online AWM beat baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the train-test gap widened. On WebArena AWM also beats SteP, which uses human-written workflows, by 7.6% relative.
quote: not always correct, thus can lead to incorrect workflows that degrade model performance
limits: Single-lab, one run per condition in the main tables as read. The cost of storing and retrieving workflows in tokens is not compared with the gain. Web navigation only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the closest accuracy evidence that storing solved routines helps later tasks of the same class. It supports a small fix library, but it adds no equal-token control and confirms the over-general risk.

source: Cemri, Pan, Yang et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Failure modes were annotated by hand in 150 traces, then an LLM judge labelled 1600+ traces from 7 frameworks. The stuck-like modes (step repetition, not recognising completion, reasoning-action mismatch) are frequent. This is the only frequency table for loop-like failures in LLM agent traces found this run. It is not a count of Soar impasse types.
numbers: 14 failure modes in 3 categories. Category shares: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. Text figures: step repetition 15.7%, not recognising task completion 12.4%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, premature termination 6.2%, no or incomplete verification 8.2%, incorrect verification 9.1%. Annotation kappa 0.88; LLM annotator 94% accuracy. Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across frameworks. A role-prompt fix gave +9.4% success on ChatDev; a topology change +15.6% on ProgramDev.
quote: Successful systems all work alike; each failing system has its own problems.
limits: Multi-agent frameworks (MetaGPT, ChatDev, AG2 and others), not single-agent reasoning scaffolds. The figure extraction was scrambled, so the percentages shown come from the paper text and may mix shares of failures with shares of traces. There is no tie or conflict category.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a rough prior that no-change-like loops (repetition, missed completion) are common at roughly 12 to 16% of failure labels, while ties and conflicts are not categories at all. The real base rate has to be counted in our own scaffold logs.

finding: A production agent uses a code-fired stuck detector with five fixed patterns. Each compares recent actions and observations, ignoring process ids. No precision or recall is reported in the file, and none was found in the docs read.
numbers: Scenario 1: same action and same observation 4 times in a row. Scenario 2: same action producing errors 3 times (with checks for repeated syntax errors). Scenario 3: monologue, the agent repeats the same message 3 times. Scenario 4: an A-B-A-B-A-B alternation over the last 6 actions and 6 observations. Scenario 5: 10 context-condensation events in a row. Detection needs at least 3 filtered events.
limits: Source code only; there is no evaluation of false alarms or misses. Thresholds (3, 4, 6, 10) look hand-chosen.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: confirms that code-fired triggers are standard practice and that our 'same error twice' threshold is more aggressive than the 3 and 4 in a widely used agent. Nobody measured how often these fire on slow-but-progressing runs. We must log false alarms ourselves.

source: Fan, Li, Sun, Zhou (2025) Missing Premise exacerbates Overthinking
finding: On ill-posed questions with a missing premise, reasoning models produce far more tokens and mostly fail to say the question cannot be answered. Non-reasoning models answer in similar length for both kinds of question and detect the problem sooner. Overthinking spreads through distillation.
numbers: QwQ-32B and DeepSeek-R1 go from about 1,000 tokens on simple GSM8K questions to more than 3,000 under a missing premise, 2x to 4x more. On well-defined questions non-reasoning models need about 200 tokens versus 1,000 for R1 and 1,800 for QwQ-32B. Most reasoning models do not abstain correctly; GPT-o1 is the exception named.
quote: the response length of reasoning LLMs ... drastically increases for ill-posed questions with missing premises
limits: Missing premises, not contradictory constraints; GPT-4o used as grader. No test of a dedicated fallback operator.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a model left to think more on an unsolvable problem does not reach a stop-and-flag state. Keep a code-fired budget cap and an explicit 'constraints cannot all hold' exit; more preferences or more thinking will not reliably end it. Seeded contradiction tests are still needed.

source: Wang, Liu, Xu et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models switch between lines of thought too often on wrong answers. Wrong answers are longer and contain more thought switches than right ones. A decoding penalty on switch words (TIP) raised accuracy without training.
numbers: AIME2024 Table 1 underthinking score (token inefficiency in incorrect answers; higher means more underthinking): QwQ-32B-Preview 65.0, DeepSeek-R1-Preview 75.7, DeepSeek-R1-671B 37.0. Accuracy 46.7, 46.7 and 73.3. MATH500-Hard: R1-671B 92.5 accuracy, 65.4 score. GPQA Diamond: R1-671B 73.2 accuracy, 58.8 score.
quote: frequently switch between different reasoning thoughts without sufficiently exploring promising paths
limits: Open reasoning models only, decoding-time intervention, not a scaffold. The score depends on an LLM judge splitting thoughts.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 10: model-side 'try something else' signals are noisy and often wrong. A switch is not evidence of an impasse. This supports firing impasse operators from code-visible events rather than from the model's own wording, and cutting premature switching.

source: Muennighoff, Yang, Shi et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing is a token cap that ends thinking and makes the model answer. The paper notes that capping at about 30,000 thinking tokens helps because the model can finish with a best guess when stuck in a loop. Suppressing the stop too often leads to repetitive loops.
numbers: Table 2 caption: scores use budget forcing at a cap of about 30,000 thinking tokens and are slightly better than the Table 1 scores without it. s1-32B with the cap: 56.7 on AIME24, 93.0 on MATH500, 59.6 on GPQA Diamond. The exact uncapped numbers were not read. AIME24 has 30 questions, so one question is 3.3 points. Pushing 'Wait' extends thinking and flattens after about six times.
quote: allows the model to finish with a best guess when stuck in an infinite loop
limits: Single-stream reasoning, not nested subgoals. AIME24 has N=30. Not measured against an uncapped run at equal total tokens; the 'slightly better' claim is from the caption.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: weak support for a hard cap with a forced best-guess answer, the same fallback Laird describes. It does not tell us what depth cap suits recursive subgoals.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Only the abstract and first pages of the PDF text were read this session. The survey concludes that no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs except in tasks that are exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works well where reliable external feedback exists, and large-scale fine-tuning enables it. It adds that many studies use oracle information or weak baselines that overstate gains.
numbers: No pooled effect size; a survey. It provides a checklist for fair evaluation of self-correction.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Partly read. A review, so its claim depends on the papers it chose.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: a recovery operator is credible when its feedback comes from code or tools (our design) and is shaky when it is the model judging itself. Run the equal-token control with an oracle-free baseline, as the survey's checklist asks.

source: Citation lookup for NL2GenSym (arXiv 2510.09355) via Semantic Scholar API
finding: Negative result for Gap 6. The citation list returned empty (data: []). An arXiv API title search for the CogRec, NL2GenSym and Soar-impasse-LLM terms returned only the original papers. The CogRec citation lookup and the OpenAlex search were refused with HTTP 429, and the web search budget was used up.
numbers: NL2GenSym citations returned: 0. arXiv search hits for NL2GenSym: 1 (itself). For CogRec plus Soar: 1 (itself). Soar plus impasse plus language: 1 (CogRec).
limits: Absence in a citation index that lags months behind and was only partly reachable is weak evidence. Could not check CogRec, STARS or Google Scholar.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Treat all three results as unreplicated single-lab claims, as the critique says.

source: Laird, Newell, Rosenbloom (1987) SOAR: An architecture for general intelligence; Laird (2012) The Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Not read again. The guessed UMich PDF address returned a certificate error, the Soar site paths tried returned 404, and Semantic Scholar was rate-limited when asked for an open-access link. Nothing new about universal subgoaling or the eight-step decision procedure can be added from these two works.
limits: Access failure, not an absence of content.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. A person with library access should read the 1987 paper section on universal subgoaling.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, as used in Snell et al. and Kamoi et al. (cross-read)
finding: Cross-reference only: both Snell et al. (revision needs a verifier to avoid breaking correct answers, 38%) and Kamoi et al. (self-correction needs reliable external feedback) agree with the earlier Huang et al. finding that intrinsic self-correction does not help. Three independent papers point to the same boundary condition.
numbers: See d03 for the 38% figure; Huang et al. numbers are in evidence_a.
limits: Not re-opened here; shown only to mark the convergence.
agent_relevance: Strengthens the design choice that checks come from code, not from the model's own judgment (G7).

source: Synthesis of d01, d03, d04, d05, d06 for Gap 4 and Gap 2
finding: Ordering of the evidence on isolation: Laban shows that carried-over failed attempts hurt and that restating facts recovers only 15 to 20% of the loss; Snell shows revision conditioned on earlier attempts breaks 38% of correct answers; Context-Folding and THREAD show that returning a short result from a separate context works, with no equal-token ablation. None changes only the isolation factor.
limits: Inference across papers with different tasks, models and cost measures. Not a test.
agent_relevance: The isolation test (fresh context returning a typed result against shared context, at equal tokens) is a clean, cheap experiment that fills a hole in all five papers.
